column4: The clear victory is the concrete opening gift of the sentence whose next ayah says God's favor to the Prophet will be completed; it identifies one historical form of that completion.
God's mighty help completes the sequence of forgiveness, completed favor, and guidance in 48:2; the ayah contributes the protective support toward which the promise proceeds.
The Messenger's reciting, purifying, and teaching supplies the staged means by which the favor and guidance promised in 2:150 reach the community.
Immediately after the completed-favor passage, God commands remembrance and gratitude and forbids ingratitude; it states the recipient's answer to the completed gift.
The Book given to Moses is described as a completion for the one who did good, a detailed exposition, guidance, and mercy; completion and guidance are again aspects of one delivered good.
God tells Moses that He had bestowed favor on him once before, explicitly introducing the remembered sequence that culminates in the eye-delight and appointed arrival of 20:40.
Inspiring Moses' mother is the first concrete act within the former favor announced in 20:37; the completed rescue begins as hidden direction.
The chest, river, divinely cast love, and rearing under God's eye show protective care operating through danger before the reunion narrated in 20:40.

God tells Moses' mother to nurse him, cast him into the river without fear, and trust the promise to return him and make him a messenger; the whole favor is announced from peril to its distant completion.
God's preventing Moses from accepting other nurses allows his sister to direct Pharaoh's household back to his family; this ayah contributes the concealed mechanism completed in 28:13.
At recognition Joseph says God has favored him and his brother and links that outcome to reverence and patience; the early promise of completed family favor is acknowledged within its fulfillment.
After the reunion, Joseph recounts the kingdom and dream-knowledge God gave him and addresses God as his guardian in both worlds; received favor is spoken at the story's completed end.
The person promised eventual satisfaction in 92:21 gives wealth for purification; the ayah shows conveyed good as the action within the promise's movement.
Seeking only the face of his Lord gives the giver's stance immediately before “he will surely be pleased”; satisfaction is oriented to the Lord rather than repayment by people.
The question whether a human simply has whatever he desires sets a boundary on wish and entitlement; 53:25 answers that first and last belong to God.
God tells the Prophet that He has given him al-Kawthar, an abundant good; it is a direct fulfilled counterpart to the Lord's promise to give in 93:5.
The command to pray and sacrifice to one's Lord follows the abundant gift in 108:1, modeling an enacted response after favor has been announced.
The straight path is identified as the path of those upon whom God has bestowed favor; favor and guidance are inseparable in the Quran's opening prayer.
God's favor to the believers is the sending of a messenger who recites, purifies, and teaches them after evident error; the benefit advances them through an ordered sequence of guidance.
Moses challenges Pharaoh's claim that raising him was a favor by pointing to Pharaoh's enslavement of Israel; it exposes the moral limit of calling child-rearing a benefaction.
God could turn the crop into dry debris after people sow it; this continuation of 56:63-64 marks the dependence and reversibility of a cultivated blessing.
Abraham names the Lord who created him and guides him, beginning a first-person catalogue of care that moves through life's successive needs.
Feeding and giving drink are the Lord's acts in Abraham's catalogue, supplying the provision stage of sustained divine care.
“When I am ill, He heals me” contributes restoration to the same sequence, making care the repair of a damaged condition.
Causing death and then giving life extends the Lord's care beyond present provision to the final change of state.
Abraham hopes his Lord will forgive him on the Day of Judgment; the sequence ends in a hoped-for good whose completion lies in the later life.
God brings people from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, gives hearing, sight, and hearts, and states gratitude as the purpose; growth from helplessness into equipped life is a staged favor.
No one can remove harm God touches or repel good He intends, and His bounty reaches whom He wills; the ayah makes both delivery and ownership of good exclusive to God.
Creatures unable to carry their own provision are provided for by God along with human beings; sufficiency is an ongoing act of the Provider, not self-possession.
When mercy once tasted is removed, the human becomes despairing and ungrateful; it supplies the first mistaken response in the changing-condition sequence continued by 11:10-11.
The reversal of Sheba's gardens is explicitly called recompense for ingratitude; it gives the reason for the loss narrated in 34:16.
Whoever changes God's favor after it has reached them faces severe consequence; the ayah marks reception as no guarantee against corrupting the gift.
When favor reaches a human, he turns away, and when harm reaches him, he despairs; the paired reactions oppose grateful recognition of the giver.
This repeated formulation says that a favored human turns aside arrogantly but becomes full of prayer under harm; changing conditions reveal an unstable reading of favor.
After warnings are forgotten, the gates of everything are opened until the recipients exult and are seized suddenly; apparent increase can be a prelude to judgment rather than completed good.
The Prophet is told not to admire opponents' wealth and children because God may punish them through those very things; visible abundance is bounded from true favor.
The “tranquil soul” is the addressee invited to return well pleased and pleasing in 89:28; inner settledness introduces the section's true endpoint of satisfaction.
Entering among God's servants is the first realized outcome after the soul is called well pleased and pleasing.
Entering God's garden completes the sequence begun with the tranquil soul, locating satisfaction in the final bestowed home.
Eternal gardens culminate in “God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him”; reciprocal approval is the fullness of the promised good state.
God is pleased with the believers beneath the tree, sends tranquility upon them, and rewards them with a near victory; approval is accompanied by inward and outward gifts.
The believers return untouched by harm with favor and bounty from God while following His approval; favor, safety, and riḍwān occur together.
God guides those who seek His approval along paths of peace and out of darkness into light; riḍwān determines the path and its repaired condition.
The Prophet is commanded to endure and glorify his Lord through the day's turns so that he may be satisfied; it is another direct divine address promising his satisfaction.
David and Solomon publicly praise God for knowledge and for favoring them; their speech is a direct model of telling a received favor.
After being settled upon means of travel, people are commanded to remember their Lord's favor and declare His transcendence; ordinary provision becomes spoken remembrance.
The people of the Garden praise God for guiding them and confess they could not have found the path unless He guided them; completed guidance is narrated by its recipients.
Believers are told to remember God's favor when hostile people intended to seize them and He restrained their hands; protection from a concrete threat is made a narrated blessing.
Believers are commanded to remember God's favor when armies came and He sent wind and unseen forces; rescue under siege is another specific favor to be recounted.
Salih's people are told to remember being settled in the land with palaces and mountain homes and to remember God's benefits; habitation and shaped land are favors demanding recognition.
People are told to eat lawful good provision and to thank God's favor; provision received and gratitude are explicitly paired.
Believers are commanded to eat the good things God provided and thank Him; delivered good becomes the immediate ground of gratitude.
David's household is commanded to work in gratitude after the kingdom's extraordinary provisions, while few servants are grateful; thanks is an active use of favor.
Worldly life is pictured as vegetation that pleases and then withers, while the Hereafter holds punishment, forgiveness, and riḍwān; transient increase is set against enduring approval.
Worldly possessions are temporary enjoyment and adornment, whereas what is with God is better and more enduring; it directly restates the later-good comparison.
One who meets a good promise is contrasted with one briefly given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment; fulfilled promise and passing gift are sharply separated.
Captives are promised that if God knows good in their hearts, He will give them something better than what was taken and forgive them; loss can be carried to a superior divine replacement.
The two servants intend that the child's parents receive from their Lord a replacement better in purity and nearer in mercy; hidden care may complete itself through a good not yet visible.
People may dislike something in which God places abundant good; present perception therefore does not exhaust the good being brought about.
People may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad while God knows and they do not; it sets an epistemic boundary on reading present conditions as favor or harm.
Referring disputes to God and the Messenger is called better and best in outcome; khayr and taʾwīl meet in an ordered return to the final meaning.
Full measure and a straight balance are called better and best in outcome; completion, right ordering, khayr, and the root of taʾwīl converge in a concrete transaction.
A goodly loan to God is multiplied many times; benefit advanced to another returns as divinely increased good.
God destroys usury and causes charities to grow; the ayah directly distinguishes extractive increase from increase attached to conveyed good.
The goodly loan is promised multiplication and a noble reward; generosity opens into increase from God.
Men and women who give charity and lend a goodly loan receive multiplication and noble reward; the repeated formula applies increasing good to both.
A goodly loan is multiplied and joined to forgiveness; increase and repair complete the good passed onward.
Creation proceeds from dust and a drop through childhood, maturity, old age, and an appointed term; the ayah supplies an explicit state-to-state progression under divine agency.
Water sent from the sky becomes drink and vegetation on which animals graze; divine provision begins the estate's movement from water to use.
The same water grows crops, olives, palms, grapes, and every fruit; the cultivated benefit develops into completed variety.
Luqman receives wisdom with the charge to thank God, and gratitude benefits its practitioner; a received gift is answered by recognition.
Worldly enjoyment is called little and the Hereafter better for the reverent; it repeats the section's comparative judgment in a warning against attachment to the near life.
Worldly life is play and diversion, while the home of the Hereafter is better for the reverent; the better later state is contrasted with passing activity.
Heirs to scripture grasp the goods of the lower life while presuming forgiveness, then are reminded that the later home is better for the reverent; “better” corrects compromised desire.
After Joseph's authority and mercy in this world, the reward of the Hereafter is called better for believers; his realized favor remains open to a superior later good.
Those who answer that their Lord sent good receive good here, and the home of the Hereafter is better; one divine good advances into another superior state.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment, while enduring good deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope; lasting good displaces possession as the desired end.
Those given knowledge tell the admirers of Qarun that God's reward is better for the faithful who do good; the claim corrects the crowd's reading of visible wealth.
What people receive is temporary worldly enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for believers who trust Him.
Those clinging to the ground are asked whether they are satisfied with worldly life instead of the Hereafter, whose comparison makes present enjoyment very small.
